1	# McpFn architecture
     2	
     3	McpFn separates protocol correctness from product correctness and gives every
     4	client-side tool one session engine.
     5	
     6	```text
     7	MCP client
     8	   |
     9	official MCP SDK transports and protocol lifecycle
    10	   |
    11	OAuth resource-server wrapper -> validated authInfo
    12	   |
    13	McpFnServer -> trusted request context and client-mediated requests
    14	   |
    15	McpFnRegistry -> tools/resources/prompts/tasks -> domain handlers
    16	   |                                      |
    17	explicit domain tool                 DatafnExecutor
    18	                                          |
    19	                             DataFn auth, namespace, policy,
    20	                             hooks, rate limits, idempotency
    21	
    22	application / CLI / test / inspector
    23	   |
    24	McpFnClient capability facades and lifecycle diagnostics
    25	   |
    26	McpFnTarget: stdio | Streamable HTTP | custom
    27	   |
    28	official MCP SDK client transports and OAuth orchestration
    29	```
    30	
    31	## Runtime ownership
    32	
    33	The official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` owns initialization, JSON-RPC dispatch, stdio framing, Streamable HTTP, capability negotiation, ping, and protocol errors. McpFn does not carry a second MCP protocol implementation.
    34	
    35	`McpFnServer` owns server identity, capability derivation, request-context construction, pagination, dispatch, error normalization, client-mediated roots/sampling/elicitation, notifications, and transport connection lifecycle. One `McpFnServer` instance connects to one transport. A host accepting multiple connections creates one server instance per connection while sharing the immutable registry.
    36	
    37	`McpFnRegistry` owns the application contract. It registers tools, exact resources, URI-template resources, prompts, completions, subscriptions, and task-capable tool handlers. Ajv validates tool and prompt inputs. URI templates are parsed once at registration. Task-capable tools require an explicit SDK `TaskStore`. MCP App links are validated across the full registry before a server or manifest is created.
    38	
    39	`McpFnServerDeclaration` is the side-effect-free application facade. It owns a
    40	registry, identity, transports, extensions, and client requirements; the same
    41	declaration creates manifests and per-connection server runtimes. Existing
    42	`McpFnServer` construction remains supported.
    43	
    44	## Client and session ownership
    45	
    46	`@mcpfn/client` owns target description, connection state, initialization,
    47	complete inventory pagination, tool/resource/prompt/task facades, explicit
    48	authorization callback completion, explicit reconnection, and bounded redacted
    49	diagnostics. It uses official SDK transports and protocol objects. It may retry
    50	connection establishment when configured; it never replays a caller's tool or
    51	other capability operation.
    52	
    53	The testing package wraps this production client for in-memory and external
    54	targets. The inspector records its diagnostics and invokes its facades. The CLI
    55	constructs its stdio or HTTP targets. This one-way dependency rule prevents
    56	test-only, inspector-only, or command-line protocol forks.
    57	
    58	## Authorization ownership
    59	
    60	The official SDK owns RFC discovery, DCR, PKCE construction, token exchange,
    61	refresh, and transport challenge handling. `@mcpfn/auth` supplies secure state
    62	and integration policy:
    63	
    64	- exact redirect matching with only the RFC 8252 loopback-port exception;
    65	- callback-state correlation before token exchange;
    66	- memory-only credentials by default or application-supplied encrypted storage;
    67	- redacted, bounded diagnostics and read-only discovery probes;
    68	- protected-resource verification and conversion to trusted SDK `authInfo`;
    69	- hosted metadata, registration, and authorization-request compatibility while
    70	  login, consent, signing, token issuance, and durable identity stay with the
    71	  host application.
    72	
    73	Client ID Metadata Document fetching is HTTPS-only, size-bounded, and requires
    74	an application allow-policy before any external URL is fetched. Additional
    75	advertised grant types do not invalidate a client that supports the requested
    76	authorization-code flow.
    77	
    78	## Manifest compatibility
    79	
    80	`createManifest` emits code-unit-sorted tool, resource, template, and prompt inventories plus a SHA-256 hash over a canonically ordered JSON representation. Object-valued capabilities, client requirements, and extensions retain their supplied insertion order in the returned body; their order does not affect the hash. `diffManifests` classifies changes as:
    81	
    82	- `breaking`: removed tools/properties/support, narrowed input enums, widened output enums, tighter input constraints, relaxed output constraints, newly required inputs, required output additions, and any output property added to a previously closed schema;
    83	- `additive`: added tools, optional input properties, optional output properties accepted by a previously open schema, widened input enums, relaxed input constraints, and added protocol/transport support;
    84	- `behavioral`: titles, descriptions, or annotations that can alter model tool selection without changing JSON validity.
    85	
    86	The diff is deliberately structural. Semantic scenarios are still required for authorization decisions, version resolution, idempotency, side effects, error envelopes, and result meaning.
    87	
    88	## DataFn integration
    89	
    90	`DatafnServer.executor` is an in-process boundary over the same query, mutation, transaction, and search handlers used by HTTP. It preserves authorization callbacks, namespace and actor derivation, schema permissions, plugins, rate limits, payload limits, and DataFn error envelopes.
    91	
    92	`@mcpfn/datafn` consumes that executor. It never accepts tenant, principal, namespace, or DataFn `clientId` values as tool arguments. Reads default on only after a resource is explicitly exposed; writes never default on.
    93	
    94	## Security invariants
    95	
    96	- Treat names, descriptions, annotations, schemas, and output shapes as versioned public contracts.
    97	- Build trusted context from the transport/authentication layer, not model-provided arguments.
    98	- Keep `additionalProperties: false` unless unknown keys are an intentional contract.
    99	- Prefer explicit output schemas for stable consumers.
   100	- Mark destructive and read-only annotations accurately; they influence client UX but do not replace server authorization.
   101	- Do not expose DataFn fields that its resolved read/write capabilities reject.
   102	- Require OAuth resource indicators and scopes at the HTTP boundary; never infer identity from model arguments.
   103	- Treat MCP Apps as untrusted HTML and declare the narrowest CSP and permissions.
   104	- Never write authorization codes, states, verifiers, tokens, cookies, or URL
   105	  credentials to diagnostic, inspection, or test artifacts.
     1	# McpFn adoption inventory
     2	
     3	This inventory separates the shared platform release from consumer migrations.
     4	
     5	| Surface | Current owner | MCP-2 state | Migration boundary |
     6	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
     7	| Server declaration/runtime | `@mcpfn/core` | Shared registry, manifest, and official-SDK runtime available | Consumers may adopt one server at a time without changing public contracts |
     8	| Production client/session | `@mcpfn/client` | stdio, Streamable HTTP, OAuth callback completion, capabilities, tasks, and diagnostics available | Replace private clients only with consumer-specific regression evidence |
     9	| OAuth compatibility | `@mcpfn/auth` | Client, resource-server, generic provider, and hosted composition seams available | Existing identity, consent, signing, token, and provider-link systems remain authoritative |
    10	| Test/quality platform | `@mcpfn/testing` | Local/external targets, scenarios, auth matrices, host-shaped fixtures, and conformance available | Each consumer supplies domain assertions and credentials through adapters |
    11	| Inspection | `@mcpfn/inspector` and `@mcpfn/cli` | Headless snapshot, execution, timeline, scenario export, and discovery diagnostics available | Product UI is a separate consumer of the headless package |
    12	| DataFn projection | `@mcpfn/datafn` | Existing deny-by-default adapter retained | Explicit domain tools remain preferred for product workflows |
    13	
    14	The `dev` base used for MCP-2 does not contain the LangFn, MemoryFn, or ProbeFn
    15	consumer packages. Their implementations on other development lines were used
    16	only to understand required lifecycle behavior; MCP-2 does not copy, modify, or
    17	claim validation for them. Each later migration must pin its public tool and
    18	authorization contract, adopt the shared client/server surface, and add its own
    19	scenario and deployment evidence.
    20	
    21	Downstream Skillplane work consumes published McpFn packages after the guarded
    22	release sequence. This repository gate proves the shared packages, examples,
    23	packed external installation, and protocol fixtures; it does not prove a
    24	downstream deployment or hosted OAuth registration.
     1	# Migrating an MCP server to McpFn
     2	
     3	## 1. Remove hand-written protocol dispatch
     4	
     5	Keep domain handlers and schemas, but replace custom initialize, tools, resources, prompts, tasks, ping, stdio framing, and Streamable HTTP parsing with an `McpFnRegistry` and `McpFnServer`. The official SDK owns those protocol paths.
     6	
     7	## 2. Register the existing public contract
     8	
     9	Preserve tool names and descriptions unless the change is intentional. Use object JSON Schemas, declare `additionalProperties`, add accurate annotations, and add output schemas wherever consumers rely on structured results.
    10	
    11	Handlers should return MCP `CallToolResult` values. `structuredResult` emits both `structuredContent` and an equivalent JSON text block. Existing domain errors with a string `code` retain that code. Use `handleInvalidArguments` only when a package has an established validation envelope that must remain stable.
    12	
    13	## 3. Build trusted context
    14	
    15	Use `createMcpFnServer({ context })` to derive principals, workspace/tenant IDs, credentials, and request metadata from authenticated transport state. Never copy these values out of tool arguments.
    16	
    17	## 4. Adopt the shared production client
    18	
    19	Replace private stdio/HTTP clients with `McpFnClient` targets. Use
    20	`McpFnTestClient` for local fixtures and `runMcpFnTargetSuite` for external
    21	targets; both route through the same production session. Assert the real
    22	initialize and capability boundary, not `registry.callTool` or handler
    23	functions alone.
    24	
    25	## 5. Commit the regression contract
    26	
    27	Generate a manifest, review it, add semantic scenarios, and run official conformance for the deployed Streamable HTTP endpoint. Put manifest diff and scenarios in required CI.
    28	
    29	## 6. Add HTTP authorization deliberately
    30	
    31	Wrap the Web Standard handler with `@mcpfn/auth` when the endpoint is protected.
    32	Supply an SDK-compatible token verifier, resource identifier,
    33	authorization-server URLs, and required scopes. Client applications use
    34	`McpFnOAuthClientProvider`, explicitly receive both callback `code` and `state`,
    35	and choose memory-only or encrypted persistence. Hosted authorization servers
    36	compose their existing identity and token systems through the compatibility
    37	handler. Do not move outbound provider OAuth flows out of
    38	`@superfunctions/oauth-*`; MCP resource-server verification and provider
    39	account linking are separate boundaries.
    40	
    41	## 7. Declare host requirements
    42	
    43	Set `clientRequirements` for roots, sampling, or elicitation used by handlers. Add extension declarations for MCP Apps, then check the manifest against the intended host profile in CI. This turns a host capability mismatch into a pre-release failure instead of a runtime surprise.
    44	
    45	## Existing Superfunctions migrations
    46	
    47	LangFn, MemoryFn, and ProbeFn migrations are outside this release. Their existing
    48	MCP compatibility surfaces remain unchanged until each consumer is migrated and
    49	its own regression suite is added to the release gate.
    50	
    51	Run `npm run gate:mcpfn-release` after changes to the shared McpFn runtime or its
    52	current DataFn adapter. Do not treat that gate as evidence for unmigrated consumers.

1	# `@mcpfn/client`
     2	
     3	Production MCP client and headless session engine for Node.js 18.18 or newer.
     4	It delegates protocol lifecycle and transports to the official MCP SDK, while
     5	adding target descriptors, idempotent connection lifecycle, complete inventory
     6	pagination, typed capability facades, explicit reconnect/cancellation, and
     7	secret-redacted phase diagnostics.
     8	
     9	```ts
    10	import { createMcpFnClient, streamableHttpTarget } from "@mcpfn/client";
    11	
    12	const client = createMcpFnClient({
    13	  target: streamableHttpTarget("https://api.example.com/mcp"),
    14	  diagnostics: (event) => audit.safe(event),
    15	});
    16	
    17	await client.connect();
    18	const tools = await client.tools.listAll();
    19	const result = await client.tools.call("orders_list", { limit: 20 });
    20	await client.close();
    21	```
    22	
    23	`stdioTarget()` is Node-only. `streamableHttpTarget()` uses Web Standard
    24	requests through the official SDK. Authorization is supplied through an
    25	official `OAuthClientProvider`, including the McpFn provider from
    26	`@mcpfn/auth`. When an interactive flow is required, `connect()` reports
    27	`MCPFN_AUTHORIZATION_REQUIRED`; pass the callback code to
    28	`completeAuthorization({ code, state })` and the client validates callback
    29	correlation, completes the SDK exchange, and reconnects without replaying a
    30	domain operation.
    31	
    32	McpFn retries only connection establishment when explicitly configured. It
    33	never implicitly replays tool calls, writes, or other capability operations.
     1	# McpFn Testing
     2	
     3	`@mcpfn/testing` provides deterministic MCP regression testing over the official SDK's in-memory transport. It tests the protocol boundary rather than calling handlers directly.
     4	
     5	It includes:
     6	
     7	- the production McpFn client exposed as a fixture;
     8	- exact manifest assertions across tools, resources, templates, and prompts;
     9	- resource, prompt, completion, subscription, and task client methods;
    10	- reusable API-key and OAuth resource-server regression matrices;
    11	- an in-memory authorization-code, PKCE, refresh, and revocation server;
    12	- extensible Client ID Metadata fixtures that include unrelated grant types;
    13	- optional Playwright fixtures for real redirect and consent-page coverage;
    14	- generic tools-only, full-protocol, and MCP Apps host profiles;
    15	- named ChatGPT- and Claude-shaped OAuth metadata fixtures;
    16	- one suite for in-memory, custom, stdio, and Streamable HTTP targets;
    17	- structured/text response parity checks;
    18	- declarative semantic scenarios;
    19	- orchestration of the official `@modelcontextprotocol/conformance` runner.
    20	
    21	Official conformance validates protocol behavior. McpFn scenarios validate product behavior. Production MCP servers should run both.
    22	
    23	Use `runMcpFnTargetSuite({ target, scenarios, manifest })` when a test should
    24	exercise a subprocess or deployed target. It constructs the same session used
    25	by applications, the inspector, and CLI. Scenario execution is serial and
    26	capability calls are never retried implicitly.
    27	
    28	```ts
    29	import {
    30	  McpFnTestClient,
    31	  assertManifestContract,
    32	  runScenarios,
    33	} from "@mcpfn/testing";
    34	
    35	const server = createServer();
    36	const client = await McpFnTestClient.connect(server);
    37	try {
    38	  await assertManifestContract(client, server.manifest());
    39	  const results = await runScenarios(client, [
    40	    {
    41	      name: "returns one skill",
    42	      tool: "skill_get",
    43	      arguments: { slug: "work-linear-issue" },
    44	      expect: { isError: false, structuredTextParity: true },
    45	    },
    46	  ]);
    47	  if (results.some((result) => result.status === "failed")) {
    48	    throw new Error(JSON.stringify(results));
    49	  }
    50	} finally {
    51	  await client.close();
    52	}
    53	```
    54	
    55	Scenarios run serially so stateful workflows and idempotency checks remain deterministic. `assertStructuredTextParity` requires a JSON text block; do not use it for intentionally human-readable text.
    56	
    57	`checkHostCompatibility(manifest, profile)` returns `compatible`, `degraded`, or `incompatible`. Unsupported optional server surfaces are degraded; missing protocol overlap or required client-mediated features are incompatible. The built-in profiles are stable capability fixtures, not claims about the current behavior of named commercial hosts. Supply a custom profile for a captured host version.
    58	
    59	## Authentication regression suite
    60	
    61	Import the transport-level testkit from `@mcpfn/testing/auth`. The application adapter owns only credential issuance and revocation; McpFn owns the common rejection and lifecycle matrix.
    62	
    63	```ts
    64	import {
    65	  apiKeyCredential,
    66	  assertAuthRegressionSuite,
    67	  createFetchAuthTarget,
    68	} from "@mcpfn/testing/auth";
    69	
    70	await assertAuthRegressionSuite({
    71	  kind: "api-key",
    72	  target: createFetchAuthTarget({ url: "http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp" }),
    73	  invalidCredentialHeaders: { "x-api-key": "invalid" },
    74	  provider: {
    75	    capabilities: { revocation: true },
    76	    async issue() {
    77	      const key = await skillplaneTestAuth.issueApiKey();
    78	      return apiKeyCredential(key.value, { headerName: "x-api-key", scheme: "" });
    79	    },
    80	    async revoke(credential) {
    81	      await skillplaneTestAuth.revokeApiKey(credential);
    82	    },
    83	  },
    84	});
    85	```
    86	
    87	OAuth adapters can additionally enable scope, expiry, resource-binding, and revocation scenarios. Rejected OAuth requests must include a Bearer challenge with `resource_metadata`; API keys intentionally do not inherit that OAuth-specific requirement.
    88	
    89	`createOAuthClientMetadataVariants()` returns authorization-code clients with basic, JWT-bearer-extension, device-code-extension, and generic-extension metadata. The compatibility assertion requires authorization-code support while deliberately accepting unrelated grants, which catches closed-world Client ID Metadata validation regressions.
    90

async function readBoundedJson(

<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images, videos, and audio using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When an app or connector generates or edits media at a remote URL and provides a user-facing preview or display tool, use that tool instead of embedding the URL in Markdown.
- When sending or referencing a local image, video, or audio file, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When a user asks to play an audio file, render it using Markdown image syntax with an absolute path (e.g., ![audio](/absolute/path.mp3)).
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring automations, reminders, monitors, follow-ups, and thread wakeups. When the user asks to create, view, update, delete, or ask about automations, search for the `automation_update` tool first, then follow its schema instead of writing raw automation directives by hand.
- When an automation should archive a Codex thread on completion, use `set_thread_archived` instead of emitting raw archive directives.

### Thread Coordination
- Treat the terms "task", "thread", "chat", and "conversation" as synonyms when they clearly refer to Codex. Tool names use the term "thread" and Codex uses "task" in the UI. When providing user-facing responses, use "task".
- When the user asks to create, fork, inspect, continue, hand off, pin, archive, unarchive, rename, or otherwise manage Codex threads, search for the relevant thread tool first: `create_thread`, `fork_thread`, `list_threads`, `list_archived_threads`, `read_thread`, `wait_threads`, `send_message_to_thread`, `handoff_thread`, `set_thread_pinned`, `set_thread_archived`, or `set_thread_title`.
- When following another task's progress, prefer compact `wait_threads` snapshots over repeated `read_thread` calls. Use one target for single-task coordination and `timeoutMs: 0` for a compact immediate snapshot. `create_thread` dispatches asynchronously, so explicitly wait for progress. Use one bounded call for 1-8 targets with each target's `hostId` and cursor as `afterCursor`; it wakes on the first target that completes or needs attention, and timeout includes the latest commentary for all targets without waking on every commentary update. An up-to-date cursor suppresses already-delivered final text. Separate waits from one task may run serially. Do not narrate unchanged snapshots, and leave approval or user-input requests for the user.
- Only use `create_thread` when the user explicitly asks to create a new thread. You are an audit agent. Your job is to perform a THOROUGH, READ-ONLY audit of an implemented codebase against:
1) the ORIGINAL user intent/notes (authoritative source intent), AND
2) ALL spec bundles provided (SPEC/REQUIREMENTS/TEST_VECTORS/PLAN/phases/INTENT_AUDIT),
and write a comprehensive audit report to the project’s `.conduct/audits/` folder.

Authoritative inputs (VERY IMPORTANT):
- The user’s intent/notes/docs are authoritative for “what was intended”.
- The provided spec bundles are authoritative for “what was specified”.
- You MUST read ALL provided intent/notes/docs and ALL provided spec bundles thoroughly.
- Ignore any existing audit reports in `.conduct/` for the purposes of determining compliance (they may be referenced only as historical context after you complete your own independent audit).

Scope rules (no omissions allowed):
- This is a FULL audit. You MUST cover every minute detail in the original intent/notes and every requirement in every provided REQUIREMENTS.md.
- You MUST NOT reduce scope, sample, or create an MVP view of the audit.
- If multiple spec bundles conflict, do NOT pick one silently:
  - identify conflicts explicitly
  - state which bundle is treated as authoritative for “pass/fail” ONLY if the user specified precedence; otherwise mark as “SPEC CONFLICT” and recommend a resolution.
- You MUST NOT change implementation code while auditing. The only file you may create/modify is the audit report itself.

Output file (MANDATORY):
- Write the audit report to the project root’s `.conduct/audits/` folder with EXACT filename format:
  - `.conduct/audits/{yyyy-mm-dd}-{unique-id}-full-audit.md`
- `{yyyy-mm-dd}` must be the date the audit ran (format: YYYY-MM-DD).
- `{unique-id}` must be a short RANDOM alphanumeric id (example constraints: 6–10 chars, `[a-z0-9]+`).

Directory rule:
- If `.conduct/audits/` does not exist, you MUST create it.

Logging (MANDATORY, append-only):
- After writing the audit report (success or blocked), you MUST append exactly one row to:
  - `.conduct/logs.csv`
- If `.conduct/logs.csv` does not exist, you MUST create it with header row exactly:
  - `timestamp,model,launcher,command,agent_name,phase(s),path`
- The appended row MUST contain:
  - timestamp = ISO 8601 (include timezone; prefer UTC)
  - model = model name/version if known else `unknown`
  - launcher = editor/IDE name (e.g. "Cursor", "VS Code", "IntelliJ") or "CLI" if known, else `unknown`
  - command = `audit`
  - agent_name = provided by user if available else `unknown-agent`
  - phase(s) = empty
  - path = repository-relative path to the generated audit report file (e.g. `.conduct/audits/{yyyy-mm-dd}-{unique-id}-full-audit.md`); NEVER write an absolute filesystem path

Audit report required metadata (top of file, must be present):
- exact timestamp (ISO 8601, include timezone; prefer UTC)
- agent_name
- model name/version (if known)
- launcher (editor/IDE name or "CLI" if available)
- workspace/project path recorded as `repo root` or another repository-relative path only; NEVER include an absolute filesystem path
- OS + shell in sanitized form only (for example `Darwin arm64`, shell `zsh`); NEVER include hostnames, computer names, usernames, home-directory paths, or full shell executable paths
- repo metadata if available (git: branch, commit, dirty status; if not a git repo, say so)
- intent/notes paths audited, expressed as repository-relative paths when possible and otherwise as sanitized descriptors
- spec bundle paths audited (each bundle: repository-relative root path + included files; use sanitized descriptors for any external inputs)
- codebase scope audited (repository-relative root path + any excluded folders)
- commands executed during audit (if any)

Artifact portability requirements (MANDATORY):
- Do NOT write usernames, home-directory paths, hostnames, computer names, or other machine-specific identifiers into the audit report or logs.
- Do NOT write absolute filesystem paths anywhere in committed audit artifacts; use `repo root` or repository-relative paths instead.
- If commands were run from a local absolute path, rewrite them in the report using repository-relative forms that another developer can run from the checked-out repo root.

Audit method (follow exactly):
1) Intent inventory (source-of-truth intent):
   - Extract an “Intent Inventory” from the user’s notes/intent/docs: a numbered, exhaustive list of every feature, constraint, invariant, edge case, API expectation, and “must not” rule.
2) Spec inventory (what is specified):
   - For each provided spec bundle:
     - if INTENT_AUDIT.md exists, use it as a starting point but still validate it
     - enumerate all requirements from REQUIREMENTS.md (requirement IDs, statements, acceptance criteria, referenced test vectors)
3) Spec-vs-intent audit (spec completeness / drift):
   - For EACH intent item:
     - map it to where it is specified (SPEC sections + requirement IDs + test vectors)
     - if missing: mark “SPEC MISSING” (this is a failure of the spec, not necessarily the implementation)
   - Identify spec conflicts across bundles (same concept specified differently).
4) Implementation audit (code vs what was intended and specified):
   - For EACH intent item and each requirement:
     - locate implementation evidence (files/symbols/tests)
     - verify behavior (prefer running tests/vectors; otherwise static audit with explicit limitations)
     - mark status:
       - PASS / PARTIAL / FAIL / UNVERIFIED for implementation
       - SPEC MISSING / SPEC CONFLICT where applicable
5) Cross-cutting audits (must include dedicated sections):
   - Security/authz/validation boundaries (as per intent/spec)
   - Determinism invariants
   - Limits/caps
   - Error handling + canonical envelopes
   - Compatibility/versioning/migrations
6) Summarize:
   - Coverage summary across:
     - intent coverage in spec (intent→spec)
     - spec coverage in code (requirements→code)
   - Top risks (ranked; include why it matters)
   - Fix order list (ranked; reference intent item numbers + requirement IDs)

Audit report structure (use these headings):
- Metadata
- Audit scope
- Inputs audited (intent + spec bundles)
- High-level findings
- Intent Inventory (numbered)
- Intent → Spec coverage matrix (complete; no sampling)
- Requirement coverage summary (PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL/UNVERIFIED counts per spec bundle)
- Requirement-by-requirement results (tables + per-requirement notes)
- Spec conflicts / spec gaps (explicit)
- Cross-cutting audits (security/determinism/limits/errors/compat)
- Recommendations (ranked)
- Appendix: commands run + environment details

User inputs (to be provided by the user in the task using this prompt):
- agent_name = <agent_name>
- project_root = <path>
- intent_paths = <one or more paths to intent/notes/docs>
- spec_bundle_paths = <one or more paths to spec bundle folders/files>
Now run the audit and write the report file.

  - path = repository-relative path to the generated audit report file (e.g. `.conduct/audits/{yyyy-mm-dd}-{unique-id}-full-audit.md`); NEVER write an absolute filesystem path

Audit report required metadata (top of file, must be present):
- exact timestamp (ISO 8601, include timezone; prefer UTC)
- agent_name
- model name/version (if known)
- launcher (editor/IDE name or "CLI" if available)
- workspace/project path recorded as `repo root` or another repository-relative path only; NEVER include an absolute filesystem path
- OS + shell in sanitized form only (for example `Darwin arm64`, shell `zsh`); NEVER include hostnames, computer names, usernames, home-directory paths, or full shell executable paths
- repo metadata if available (git: branch, commit, dirty status; if not a git repo, say so)
- intent/notes paths audited, expressed as repository-relative paths when possible and otherwise as sanitized descriptors
- spec bundle paths audited (each bundle: repository-relative root path + included files; use sanitized descriptors for any external inputs)
- codebase scope audited (repository-relative root path + any excluded folders)
- commands executed during audit (if any)

Artifact portability requirements (MANDATORY):
- Do NOT write usernames, home-directory paths, hostnames, computer names, or other machine-specific identifiers into the audit report or logs.
- Do NOT write absolute filesystem paths anywhere in committed audit artifacts; use `repo root` or repository-relative paths instead.
- If commands were run from a local absolute path, rewrite them in the report using repository-relative forms that another developer can run from the checked-out repo root.

Audit method (follow exactly):
1) Intent inventory (source-of-truth intent):
   - Extract an “Intent Inventory” from the user’s notes/intent/docs: a numbered, exhaustive list of every feature, constraint, invariant, edge case, API expectation, and “must not” rule.
2) Spec inventory (what is specified):
   - For each provided spec bundle:
     - if INTENT_AUDIT.md exists, use it as a starting point but still validate it
     - enumerate all requirements from REQUIREMENTS.md (requirement IDs, statements, acceptance criteria, referenced test vectors)
3) Spec-vs-intent audit (spec completeness / drift):
   - For EACH intent item:
     - map it to where it is specified (SPEC sections + requirement IDs + test vectors)
     - if missing: mark “SPEC MISSING” (this is a failure of the spec, not necessarily the implementation)
   - Identify spec conflicts across bundles (same concept specified differently).
4) Implementation audit (code vs what was intended and specified):
   - For EACH intent item and each requirement:
     - locate implementation evidence (files/symbols/tests)
     - verify behavior (prefer running tests/vectors; otherwise static audit with explicit limitations)
     - mark status:
       - PASS / PARTIAL / FAIL / UNVERIFIED for implementation
       - SPEC MISSING / SPEC CONFLICT where applicable
5) Cross-cutting audits (must include dedicated sections):
   - Security/authz/validation boundaries (as per intent/spec)
   - Determinism invariants
   - Limits/caps
   - Error handling + canonical envelopes
   - Compatibility/versioning/migrations
6) Summarize:
   - Coverage summary across:
     - intent coverage in spec (intent→spec)
     - spec coverage in code (requirements→code)
   - Top risks (ranked; include why it matters)
   - Fix order list (ranked; reference intent item numbers + requirement IDs)

Audit report structure (use these headings):
- Metadata
- Audit scope
- Inputs audited (intent + spec bundles)
- High-level findings
- Intent Inventory (numbered)
- Intent → Spec coverage matrix (complete; no sampling)
- Requirement coverage summary (PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL/UNVERIFIED counts per spec bundle)
- Requirement-by-requirement results (tables + per-requirement notes)
- Spec conflicts / spec gaps (explicit)
- Cross-cutting audits (security/determinism/limits/errors/compat)
- Recommendations (ranked)
- Appendix: commands run + environment details

User inputs (to be provided by the user in the task using this prompt):
- agent_name = <agent_name>
- project_root = <path>
- intent_paths = <one or more paths to intent/notes/docs>
- spec_bundle_paths = <one or more paths to spec bundle folders/files>
Now run the audit and write the report file.

{"id":"MCP-2","title":"Make McpFn the batteries-included MCP SDK and quality platform","description":"## Executive summary

Evolve McpFn from its current server-runtime and test-harness foundation into the batteries-included MCP application SDK and quality platform for Superfunctions. An application should be able to add a production MCP server or client with a small, typed McpFn integration, then use the same McpFn engine for deterministic regression coverage, official conformance, diagnostics, and a future interactive inspector.

This is a product-direction issue, not an OAuth hotfix. It preserves the official MCP SDK as the protocol implementation, composes existing Superfunctions/AuthFn boundaries where they fit, and makes MCP-specific discovery, authorization interoperability, connection lifecycle, testing, and inspection first-class McpFn responsibilities.

**Role 3 ownership decision:** McpFn owns the MCP-specific authorization-server compatibility layer presented by hosted MCP servers: protected-resource and authorization-server discovery, pre-registration/DCR/Client ID Metadata Document normalization, compatible-flow negotiation, redirect validation, PKCE/resource/scope requirements, and MCP-shaped authorization errors. AuthFn or an external authorization system continues to own identities, login, sessions, consent policy, signing keys, token authority, and durable security state.

## Problem or opportunity

The current code establishes a substantial foundation:

* `@mcpfn/core` provides an official-SDK server runtime, registry, tools/resources/prompts/tasks, MCP Apps contracts, canonical manifests, compatibility diffing, request-derived context, and stdio/Streamable HTTP support.
* `@mcpfn/auth` provides RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, bearer verification, audience/resource checks, and scope enforcement.
* `@mcpfn/testing` provides an in-memory test client, manifest assertions, semantic scenarios, auth matrices, a mock OAuth authorization server, a browser PKCE fixture, generic host profiles, and the pinned official conformance runner.
* `@mcpfn/cli` exposes manifest, validate, diff, test, and conformance commands.
* `@mcpfn/datafn` generates deny-by-default DataFn-backed tools.
* LangFn, MemoryFn, ProbeFn, and Super Console demonstrate server-side consumption on `next`; the open `dev` port deliberately excludes several consumer migrations from its release proof.

That foundation does not yet satisfy the intended McpFn product contract:

* there is no production McpFn client SDK; `McpFnTestClient` is in-memory and coupled to `McpFnServer`;
* LangFn therefore carries its own official-SDK client, HTTP/stdio transports, pagination, result normalization, connection lifecycle, and error mapping;
* `@mcpfn/auth` intentionally stops at the resource-server boundary and does not perform protected-resource discovery, authorization-server selection, client registration/metadata negotiation, PKCE, browser handoff, callback validation, token exchange/refresh/revocation, or secure token persistence;
* current OAuth fixtures validate a controlled happy path but do not model enough provider- and host-shaped redirect, discovery, registration, and metadata behavior to catch the recent `redirect_uri is not registered for this client` class of regression early;
* regression commands are primarily McpFn-native/in-memory today, while transport-neutral external-server work is separately tracked by <issue id="6283bb40-0de7-4875-a6f1-31a5016044c8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing">MCP-1</issue>;
* the documentation explicitly places product-level inspector/evaluation UIs outside the current scope;
* Super Console's MCP page inventories administrative tools and clients but is not an interactive MCP protocol inspector.

The opportunity is to make these pieces one coherent platform instead of requiring each consumer to assemble production client behavior, OAuth interoperability, test adapters, diagnostics, and inspection independently.

## Expected outcome

A TypeScript application can:

1. declare and serve a protocol-correct MCP surface with a concise McpFn server SDK;
2. connect to local or remote MCP servers with a production McpFn client SDK;
3. enable MCP-specific OAuth discovery and authorization with safe defaults and explicit policy hooks;
4. compose AuthFn or another identity/authorization system without reimplementing generic user authentication;
5. run the same manifest, semantic, auth, transport, and official-conformance engine in tests and CI;
6. inspect a connection interactively through a future McpFn inspector that consumes the same client/session/diagnostic contracts.

Consumer-owned domain semantics, tenancy, permissions, secrets, and approval policy remain explicit.

## Goals

* Define a stable, minimal client/server developer experience and package model.
* Add a production client runtime for stdio and Streamable HTTP, including capability negotiation, pagination, lifecycle, notifications, client-mediated features, typed result/error handling, cancellation, and reconnect policy.
* Add MCP-specific OAuth client orchestration: protected-resource discovery, authorization-server metadata, supported client registration/metadata modes, PKCE, browser handoff, callback validation, resource indicators, token exchange/refresh/revocation, and pluggable secure persistence.
* Define a provider-neutral server auth seam plus first-class AuthFn/shared-OAuth adapters; keep AuthFn optional.
* Add a hosted-server authorization adapter so applications such as Skillplane delegate MCP-specific client registration, metadata compatibility, redirect matching, and authorization-request validation to McpFn instead of retaining product-local implementations.
* Reuse the official MCP SDK and Superfunctions OAuth/storage primitives instead of creating parallel protocol, state, token, or encryption implementations.
* Generalize the test client into a shared target/session engine usable by in-memory, stdio, remote HTTP, CLI, CI, and the future inspector.
* Add provider- and host-shaped deterministic interoperability profiles that cover redirect URI registration, loopback callbacks, metadata extensions, issuer/resource validation, refresh/revocation, and negative paths.
* Keep official MCP conformance complementary to McpFn contract, semantic, auth, and product smoke coverage.
* Provide redacted, structured diagnostics that identify whether a failure occurred during discovery, registration, authorization, callback, token exchange, MCP initialization, capability negotiation, or a product scenario.
* Establish a phased inspector roadmap built on the shared engine rather than a separate implementation.
* Publish migration paths for current Superfunctions consumers and verify installed-package behavior in release automation.

## Non-goals

* Reimplement JSON-RPC, MCP lifecycle, transports, or the official MCP conformance suite.
* Make AuthFn mandatory or duplicate its user/session/plugin model.
* Treat AuthFn's social-login OAuth client as an MCP authorization server.
* Reimplement generic user identity, login, sessions, consent policy, signing-key management, or durable token authority inside McpFn; these remain AuthFn, application, or external-authorization-system responsibilities.
* Require McpFn to ship a standalone generic authorization server when an adapter over an existing token authority can satisfy the hosted MCP contract.
* Auto-expose an application's domain model, infer permissions, or move tenancy/authorization policy into tool arguments.
* Promise every MCP host or authorization provider behaves identically.
* Treat a green unit, conformance, or mock-browser suite as proof of live deployment interoperability.
* Deliver the full inspector UI in the first implementation phase.
* Migrate Skillplane or other consumers inside this issue; consumer adoption remains separately tracked.

## Acceptance criteria

* A documented package/API decision defines the stable roles of core, server, client, auth, testing, CLI, adapters, and future inspector surfaces.
* A minimal server example and a minimal client example each require only application configuration, domain handlers, and explicit policy hooks—not hand-written MCP lifecycle code.
* The production client connects over stdio and Streamable HTTP and exercises tools, resources, prompts, tasks, notifications, and negotiated client-mediated features through the official SDK.
* The client supports MCP authorization discovery through a pluggable OAuth lifecycle and storage contract, with structured phase-specific errors and redacted diagnostics.
* OAuth regression coverage includes fixed web callbacks, native/loopback callbacks with dynamic ports, exact registered redirect handling, client metadata/DCR variants, PKCE/state replay protection, issuer/resource checks, token endpoint auth-method negotiation, refresh rotation, revocation, denial, expiry, and unsupported-grant classification.
* The recent redirect-registration failure class is reproducible as a deterministic regression that fails when generated authorization requests and registered client metadata diverge.
* A hosted MCP server can delegate all MCP-specific authorization interoperability to McpFn while supplying identity, consent, authorization policy, signing, and storage adapters; consumer code does not parse client metadata, negotiate registration modes, compare redirect URIs, enforce PKCE, or map MCP-specific authorization errors.
* Independently configured Claude-shaped and ChatGPT-shaped end-to-end fixtures complete valid authorization-code + PKCE flows; deliberately incompatible metadata and unregistered callbacks fail with phase-accurate errors.
* The implementation inventories overlapping McpFn, LangFn, shared OAuth, AuthFn, and consumer authorization code; generic PKCE/state/HTTP/storage/redaction primitives are reused, and replaced product-local paths are removed or explicitly deprecated with no parallel production writer.
* McpFn exposes a documented AuthFn integration that maps authenticated subjects/scopes into trusted server context while leaving token issuance/authorization-server policy behind an explicit adapter.
* Generic OAuth state, transport, and encrypted token-storage behavior is reused from the shared Superfunctions packages where compatible; any MCP-specific fork is justified in the architecture document.
* The same target/session engine supports McpFn-native in-memory tests and transport-neutral stdio/HTTP targets without requiring external servers to adopt McpFn server types.
* CLI and programmatic APIs produce bounded, machine-readable, secret-redacted reports with stable exit behavior.
* <issue id="6283bb40-0de7-4875-a6f1-31a5016044c8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing">MCP-1</issue>'s external regression/conformance work plugs into the shared engine and is not duplicated.
* An inspector contract and thin initial shell can discover capabilities, run operations, observe notifications/tasks, visualize auth/discovery phases, and export a reproducible redacted test case using the same client engine.
* Release gates verify package exports, packed-package installation, representative client/server round trips, OAuth browser coverage, manifest/scenario coverage, official conformance, and explicitly named consumer coverage.
* Documentation distinguishes deterministic local proof, official conformance, provider-shaped simulations, controlled live-provider smoke tests, and deployed production proof.

## Dependencies and risks

* Related foundation: <issue id="a44566ef-0f0a-4aa5-b5fa-abe7c38032c3" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-19/mcpfn-init">SFN-19</issue>.
* Related transport-neutral testing work: <issue id="6283bb40-0de7-4875-a6f1-31a5016044c8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing">MCP-1</issue>.
* Skillplane adoption remains in <issue id="aaf7021f-756f-4919-ad1c-830c2fa250f8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-6/adopt-mcpfn-for-mcp-regression-and-conformance-coverage">SKI-6</issue>.
* The official MCP SDK and conformance runner evolve; version support and upgrade policy must be explicit.
* Browser and desktop callback environments differ in redirect and loopback behavior.
* DCR, client metadata documents, pre-registration, and enterprise-managed authorization require different policy and security postures.
* Token storage, refresh concurrency, revocation, logging, and exported inspector traces can leak credentials unless redaction and storage boundaries are designed first.
* Current `next` and the open `dev` port do not prove the same consumer coverage; release evidence must name the exact branch/package/consumer scope.
* A convenience API can accidentally obscure tenancy, authorization, confirmation, and destructive-operation controls if those hooks are not explicit.
* Package reshaping before a stable release can create migration cost; compatibility aliases and staged deprecations may be needed.
* Leaving product-local MCP authorization implementations active beside McpFn would create divergent role-3 behavior. Migration gates must verify a single production path and name every retained compatibility shim.

## Open questions

* Should the package model add `@mcpfn/client` and `@mcpfn/server`, or keep server APIs in `@mcpfn/core` with a new client package?
* Which underlying authorization-server and token-authority adapters ship first, given the fixed ownership rule that McpFn owns the MCP compatibility profile while generic identity and token authority remain external?
* Should AuthFn integration live in `@mcpfn/auth`, a dedicated adapter package, or AuthFn itself?
* Which shared OAuth primitives can be reused unchanged for MCP client authorization, and where are MCP-specific discovery/registration semantics required?
* Which runtime targets are required initially: Node only, browser, edge/Workers, desktop/native, or a staged subset?
* Is the future inspector a standalone McpFn app/package, a Super Console module, or both through a shared headless engine?
* Which named host/provider profiles are deterministic fixtures, and which live-provider checks run only on a controlled schedule?
* What compatibility guarantees apply to manifests, diagnostics, scenario files, stored credentials, and inspector exports before 1.0?

{"id":"MCP-2","title":"Make McpFn the batteries-included MCP SDK and quality platform","description":"## Executive summary

Evolve McpFn from its current server-runtime and test-harness foundation into the batteries-included MCP application SDK and quality platform for Superfunctions. An application should be able to add a production MCP server or client with a small, typed McpFn integration, then use the same McpFn engine for deterministic regression coverage, official conformance, diagnostics, and a future interactive inspector.

This is a product-direction issue, not an OAuth hotfix. It preserves the official MCP SDK as the protocol implementation, composes existing Superfunctions/AuthFn boundaries where they fit, and makes MCP-specific discovery, authorization interoperability, connection lifecycle, testing, and inspection first-class McpFn responsibilities.

**Role 3 ownership decision:** McpFn owns the MCP-specific authorization-server compatibility layer presented by hosted MCP servers: protected-resource and authorization-server discovery, pre-registration/DCR/Client ID Metadata Document normalization, compatible-flow negotiation, redirect validation, PKCE/resource/scope requirements, and MCP-shaped authorization errors. AuthFn or an external authorization system continues to own identities, login, sessions, consent policy, signing keys, token authority, and durable security state.

## Problem or opportunity

The current code establishes a substantial foundation:

* `@mcpfn/core` provides an official-SDK server runtime, registry, tools/resources/prompts/tasks, MCP Apps contracts, canonical manifests, compatibility diffing, request-derived context, and stdio/Streamable HTTP support.
* `@mcpfn/auth` provides RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, bearer verification, audience/resource checks, and scope enforcement.
* `@mcpfn/testing` provides an in-memory test client, manifest assertions, semantic scenarios, auth matrices, a mock OAuth authorization server, a browser PKCE fixture, generic host profiles, and the pinned official conformance runner.
* `@mcpfn/cli` exposes manifest, validate, diff, test, and conformance commands.
* `@mcpfn/datafn` generates deny-by-default DataFn-backed tools.
* LangFn, MemoryFn, ProbeFn, and Super Console demonstrate server-side consumption on `next`; the open `dev` port deliberately excludes several consumer migrations from its release proof.

That foundation does not yet satisfy the intended McpFn product contract:

* there is no production McpFn client SDK; `McpFnTestClient` is in-memory and coupled to `McpFnServer`;
* LangFn therefore carries its own official-SDK client, HTTP/stdio transports, pagination, result normalization, connection lifecycle, and error mapping;
* `@mcpfn/auth` intentionally stops at the resource-server boundary and does not perform protected-resource discovery, authorization-server selection, client registration/metadata negotiation, PKCE, browser handoff, callback validation, token exchange/refresh/revocation, or secure token persistence;
* current OAuth fixtures validate a controlled happy path but do not model enough provider- and host-shaped redirect, discovery, registration, and metadata behavior to catch the recent `redirect_uri is not registered for this client` class of regression early;
* regression commands are primarily McpFn-native/in-memory today, while transport-neutral external-server work is separately tracked by <issue id="6283bb40-0de7-4875-a6f1-31a5016044c8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing">MCP-1</issue>;
* the documentation explicitly places product-level inspector/evaluation UIs outside the current scope;
* Super Console's MCP page inventories administrative tools and clients but is not an interactive MCP protocol inspector.

The opportunity is to make these pieces one coherent platform instead of requiring each consumer to assemble production client behavior, OAuth interoperability, test adapters, diagnostics, and inspection independently.

## Expected outcome

A TypeScript application can:

1. declare and serve a protocol-correct MCP surface with a concise McpFn server SDK;
2. connect to local or remote MCP servers with a production McpFn client SDK;
3. enable MCP-specific OAuth discovery and authorization with safe defaults and explicit policy hooks;
4. compose AuthFn or another identity/authorization system without reimplementing generic user authentication;
5. run the same manifest, semantic, auth, transport, and official-conformance engine in tests and CI;
6. inspect a connection interactively through a future McpFn inspector that consumes the same client/session/diagnostic contracts.

Consumer-owned domain semantics, tenancy, permissions, secrets, and approval policy remain explicit.

## Goals

* Define a stable, minimal client/server developer experience and package model.
* Add a production client runtime for stdio and Streamable HTTP, including capability negotiation, pagination, lifecycle, notifications, client-mediated features, typed result/error handling, cancellation, and reconnect policy.
* Add MCP-specific OAuth client orchestration: protected-resource discovery, authorization-server metadata, supported client registration/metadata modes, PKCE, browser handoff, callback validation, resource indicators, token exchange/refresh/revocation, and pluggable secure persistence.
* Define a provider-neutral server auth seam plus first-class AuthFn/shared-OAuth adapters; keep AuthFn optional.
* Add a hosted-server authorization adapter so applications such as Skillplane delegate MCP-specific client registration, metadata compatibility, redirect matching, and authorization-request validation to McpFn instead of retaining product-local implementations.
* Reuse the official MCP SDK and Superfunctions OAuth/storage primitives instead of creating parallel protocol, state, token, or encryption implementations.
* Generalize the test client into a shared target/session engine usable by in-memory, stdio, remote HTTP, CLI, CI, and the future inspector.
* Add provider- and host-shaped deterministic interoperability profiles that cover redirect URI registration, loopback callbacks, metadata extensions, issuer/resource validation, refresh/revocation, and negative paths.
* Keep official MCP conformance complementary to McpFn contract, semantic, auth, and product smoke coverage.
* Provide redacted, structured diagnostics that identify whether a failure occurred during discovery, registration, authorization, callback, token exchange, MCP initialization, capability negotiation, or a product scenario.
* Establish a phased inspector roadmap built on the shared engine rather than a separate implementation.
* Publish migration paths for current Superfunctions consumers and verify installed-package behavior in release automation.

## Non-goals

* Reimplement JSON-RPC, MCP lifecycle, transports, or the official MCP conformance suite.
* Make AuthFn mandatory or duplicate its user/session/plugin model.
* Treat AuthFn's social-login OAuth client as an MCP authorization server.
* Reimplement generic user identity, login, sessions, consent policy, signing-key management, or durable token authority inside McpFn; these remain AuthFn, application, or external-authorization-system responsibilities.
* Require McpFn to ship a standalone generic authorization server when an adapter over an existing token authority can satisfy the hosted MCP contract.
* Auto-expose an application's domain model, infer permissions, or move tenancy/authorization policy into tool arguments.
* Promise every MCP host or authorization provider behaves identically.
* Treat a green unit, conformance, or mock-browser suite as proof of live deployment interoperability.
* Deliver the full inspector UI in the first implementation phase.
* Migrate Skillplane or other consumers inside this issue; consumer adoption remains separately tracked.

## Acceptance criteria

* A documented package/API decision defines the stable roles of core, server, client, auth, testing, CLI, adapters, and future inspector surfaces.
* A minimal server example and a minimal client example each require only application configuration, domain handlers, and explicit policy hooks—not hand-written MCP lifecycle code.
* The production client connects over stdio and Streamable HTTP and exercises tools, resources, prompts, tasks, notifications, and negotiated client-mediated features through the official SDK.
* The client supports MCP authorization discovery through a pluggable OAuth lifecycle and storage contract, with structured phase-specific errors and redacted diagnostics.
* OAuth regression coverage includes fixed web callbacks, native/loopback callbacks with dynamic ports, exact registered redirect handling, client metadata/DCR variants, PKCE/state replay protection, issuer/resource checks, token endpoint auth-method negotiation, refresh rotation, revocation, denial, expiry, and unsupported-grant classification.
* The recent redirect-registration failure class is reproducible as a deterministic regression that fails when generated authorization requests and registered client metadata diverge.
* A hosted MCP server can delegate all MCP-specific authorization interoperability to McpFn while supplying identity, consent, authorization policy, signing, and storage adapters; consumer code does not parse client metadata, negotiate registration modes, compare redirect URIs, enforce PKCE, or map MCP-specific authorization errors.
* Independently configured Claude-shaped and ChatGPT-shaped end-to-end fixtures complete valid authorization-code + PKCE flows; deliberately incompatible metadata and unregistered callbacks fail with phase-accurate errors.
* The implementation inventories overlapping McpFn, LangFn, shared OAuth, AuthFn, and consumer authorization code; generic PKCE/state/HTTP/storage/redaction primitives are reused, and replaced product-local paths are removed or explicitly deprecated with no parallel production writer.
* McpFn exposes a documented AuthFn integration that maps authenticated subjects/scopes into trusted server context while leaving token issuance/authorization-server policy behind an explicit adapter.
* Generic OAuth state, transport, and encrypted token-storage behavior is reused from the shared Superfunctions packages where compatible; any MCP-specific fork is justified in the architecture document.
* The same target/session engine supports McpFn-native in-memory tests and transport-neutral stdio/HTTP targets without requiring external servers to adopt McpFn server types.
* CLI and programmatic APIs produce bounded, machine-readable, secret-redacted reports with stable exit behavior.
* <issue id="6283bb40-0de7-4875-a6f1-31a5016044c8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing">MCP-1</issue>'s external regression/conformance work plugs into the shared engine and is not duplicated.
* An inspector contract and thin initial shell can discover capabilities, run operations, observe notifications/tasks, visualize auth/discovery phases, and export a reproducible redacted test case using the same client engine.
* Release gates verify package exports, packed-package installation, representative client/server round trips, OAuth browser coverage, manifest/scenario coverage, official conformance, and explicitly named consumer coverage.
* Documentation distinguishes deterministic local proof, official conformance, provider-shaped simulations, controlled live-provider smoke tests, and deployed production proof.

## Dependencies and risks

* Related foundation: <issue id="a44566ef-0f0a-4aa5-b5fa-abe7c38032c3" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-19/mcpfn-init">SFN-19</issue>.
* Related transport-neutral testing work: <issue id="6283bb40-0de7-4875-a6f1-31a5016044c8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-1/enable-transport-neutral-mcpfn-regression-and-conformance-testing">MCP-1</issue>.
* Skillplane adoption remains in <issue id="aaf7021f-756f-4919-ad1c-830c2fa250f8" href="https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-6/adopt-mcpfn-for-mcp-regression-and-conformance-coverage">SKI-6</issue>.
* The official MCP SDK and conformance runner evolve; version support and upgrade policy must be explicit.
* Browser and desktop callback environments differ in redirect and loopback behavior.
* DCR, client metadata documents, pre-registration, and enterprise-managed authorization require different policy and security postures.
* Token storage, refresh concurrency, revocation, logging, and exported inspector traces can leak credentials unless redaction and storage boundaries are designed first.
* Current `next` and the open `dev` port do not prove the same consumer coverage; release evidence must name the exact branch/package/consumer scope.
* A convenience API can accidentally obscure tenancy, authorization, confirmation, and destructive-operation controls if those hooks are not explicit.
* Package reshaping before a stable release can create migration cost; compatibility aliases and staged deprecations may be needed.
* Leaving product-local MCP authorization implementations active beside McpFn would create divergent role-3 behavior. Migration gates must verify a single production path and name every retained compatibility shim.

## Open questions

* Should the package model add `@mcpfn/client` and `@mcpfn/server`, or keep server APIs in `@mcpfn/core` with a new client package?
* Which underlying authorization-server and token-authority adapters ship first, given the fixed ownership rule that McpFn owns the MCP compatibility profile while generic identity and token authority remain external?
* Should AuthFn integration live in `@mcpfn/auth`, a dedicated adapter package, or AuthFn itself?
* Which shared OAuth primitives can be reused unchanged for MCP client authorization, and where are MCP-specific discovery/registration semantics required?
* Which runtime targets are required initially: Node only, browser, edge/Workers, desktop/native, or a staged subset?
* Is the future inspector a standalone McpFn app/package, a Super Console module, or both through a shared headless engine?
* Which named host/provider profiles are deterministic fixtures, and which live-provider checks run only on a controlled schedule?
* What compatibility guarantees apply to manifests, diagnostics, scenario files, stored credentials, and inspector exports before 1.0?

1	# McpFn architecture
     2	
     3	McpFn separates protocol correctness from product correctness and gives every
     4	client-side tool one session engine.
     5	
     6	```text
     7	MCP client
     8	   |
     9	official MCP SDK transports and protocol lifecycle
    10	   |
    11	OAuth resource-server wrapper -> validated authInfo
    12	   |
    13	McpFnServer -> trusted request context and client-mediated requests
    14	   |
    15	McpFnRegistry -> tools/resources/prompts/tasks -> domain handlers
    16	   |                                      |
    17	explicit domain tool                 DatafnExecutor
    18	                                          |
    19	                             DataFn auth, namespace, policy,
    20	                             hooks, rate limits, idempotency
    21	
    22	application / CLI / test / inspector
    23	   |
    24	McpFnClient capability facades and lifecycle diagnostics
    25	   |
    26	McpFnTarget: stdio | Streamable HTTP | custom
    27	   |
    28	official MCP SDK client transports and OAuth orchestration
    29	```
    30	
    31	## Runtime ownership
    32	
    33	The official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` owns initialization, JSON-RPC dispatch, stdio framing, Streamable HTTP, capability negotiation, ping, and protocol errors. McpFn does not carry a second MCP protocol implementation.
    34	
    35	`McpFnServer` owns server identity, capability derivation, request-context construction, pagination, dispatch, error normalization, client-mediated roots/sampling/elicitation, notifications, and transport connection lifecycle. One `McpFnServer` instance connects to one transport. A host accepting multiple connections creates one server instance per connection while sharing the immutable registry.
    36	
    37	`McpFnRegistry` owns the application contract. It registers tools, exact resources, URI-template resources, prompts, completions, subscriptions, and task-capable tool handlers. Ajv validates tool and prompt inputs. URI templates are parsed once at registration. Task-capable tools require an explicit SDK `TaskStore`. MCP App links are validated across the full registry before a server or manifest is created.
    38	
    39	`McpFnServerDeclaration` is the side-effect-free application facade. It owns a
    40	registry, identity, transports, extensions, and client requirements; the same
    41	declaration creates manifests and per-connection server runtimes. Existing
    42	`McpFnServer` construction remains supported.
    43	
    44	## Client and session ownership
    45	
    46	`@mcpfn/client` owns target description, connection state, initialization,
    47	complete inventory pagination, tool/resource/prompt/task facades, explicit
    48	authorization callback completion, explicit reconnection, and bounded redacted
    49	diagnostics. It uses official SDK transports and protocol objects. It may retry
    50	connection establishment when configured; it never replays a caller's tool or
    51	other capability operation.
    52	
    53	The testing package wraps this production client for in-memory and external
    54	targets. The inspector records its diagnostics and invokes its facades. The CLI
    55	constructs its stdio or HTTP targets. This one-way dependency rule prevents
    56	test-only, inspector-only, or command-line protocol forks.
    57	
    58	## Authorization ownership
    59	
    60	The official SDK owns RFC discovery, DCR, PKCE construction, token exchange,
    61	refresh, and transport challenge handling. `@mcpfn/auth` supplies secure state
    62	and integration policy:
    63	
    64	- exact redirect matching with only the RFC 8252 loopback-port exception;
    65	- callback-state correlation before token exchange;
    66	- memory-only credentials by default or application-supplied encrypted storage;
    67	- redacted, bounded diagnostics and read-only discovery probes;
    68	- protected-resource verification and conversion to trusted SDK `authInfo`;
    69	- hosted metadata, registration, and authorization-request compatibility while
    70	  login, consent, signing, token issuance, and durable identity stay with the
    71	  host application.
    72	
    73	Client ID Metadata Document fetching is HTTPS-only, size-bounded, and requires
    74	an application allow-policy before any external URL is fetched. Additional
    75	advertised grant types do not invalidate a client that supports the requested
    76	authorization-code flow.
    77	
    78	## Manifest compatibility
    79	
    80	`createManifest` emits code-unit-sorted tool, resource, template, and prompt inventories plus a SHA-256 hash over a canonically ordered JSON representation. Object-valued capabilities, client requirements, and extensions retain their supplied insertion order in the returned body; their order does not affect the hash. `diffManifests` classifies changes as:
    81	
    82	- `breaking`: removed tools/properties/support, narrowed input enums, widened output enums, tighter input constraints, relaxed output constraints, newly required inputs, required output additions, and any output property added to a previously closed schema;
    83	- `additive`: added tools, optional input properties, optional output properties accepted by a previously open schema, widened input enums, relaxed input constraints, and added protocol/transport support;
    84	- `behavioral`: titles, descriptions, or annotations that can alter model tool selection without changing JSON validity.
    85	
    86	The diff is deliberately structural. Semantic scenarios are still required for authorization decisions, version resolution, idempotency, side effects, error envelopes, and result meaning.
    87	
    88	## DataFn integration
    89	
    90	`DatafnServer.executor` is an in-process boundary over the same query, mutation, transaction, and search handlers used by HTTP. It preserves authorization callbacks, namespace and actor derivation, schema permissions, plugins, rate limits, payload limits, and DataFn error envelopes.
    91	
    92	`@mcpfn/datafn` consumes that executor. It never accepts tenant, principal, namespace, or DataFn `clientId` values as tool arguments. Reads default on only after a resource is explicitly exposed; writes never default on.
    93	
    94	## Security invariants
    95	
    96	- Treat names, descriptions, annotations, schemas, and output shapes as versioned public contracts.
    97	- Build trusted context from the transport/authentication layer, not model-provided arguments.
    98	- Keep `additionalProperties: false` unless unknown keys are an intentional contract.
    99	- Prefer explicit output schemas for stable consumers.
   100	- Mark destructive and read-only annotations accurately; they influence client UX but do not replace server authorization.
   101	- Do not expose DataFn fields that its resolved read/write capabilities reject.
   102	- Require OAuth resource indicators and scopes at the HTTP boundary; never infer identity from model arguments.
   103	- Treat MCP Apps as untrusted HTML and declare the narrowest CSP and permissions.
   104	- Never write authorization codes, states, verifiers, tokens, cookies, or URL
   105	  credentials to diagnostic, inspection, or test artifacts.
     1	# McpFn adoption inventory
     2	
     3	This inventory separates the shared platform release from consumer migrations.
     4	
     5	| Surface | Current owner | MCP-2 state | Migration boundary |
     6	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
     7	| Server declaration/runtime | `@mcpfn/core` | Shared registry, manifest, and official-SDK runtime available | Consumers may adopt one server at a time without changing public contracts |
     8	| Production client/session | `@mcpfn/client` | stdio, Streamable HTTP, OAuth callback completion, capabilities, tasks, and diagnostics available | Replace private clients only with consumer-specific regression evidence |
     9	| OAuth compatibility | `@mcpfn/auth` | Client, resource-server, generic provider, and hosted composition seams available | Existing identity, consent, signing, token, and provider-link systems remain authoritative |
    10	| Test/quality platform | `@mcpfn/testing` | Local/external targets, scenarios, auth matrices, host-shaped fixtures, and conformance available | Each consumer supplies domain assertions and credentials through adapters |
    11	| Inspection | `@mcpfn/inspector` and `@mcpfn/cli` | Headless snapshot, execution, timeline, scenario export, and discovery diagnostics available | Product UI is a separate consumer of the headless package |
    12	| DataFn projection | `@mcpfn/datafn` | Existing deny-by-default adapter retained | Explicit domain tools remain preferred for product workflows |
    13	
    14	The `dev` base used for MCP-2 does not contain the LangFn, MemoryFn, or ProbeFn
    15	consumer packages. Their implementations on other development lines were used
    16	only to understand required lifecycle behavior; MCP-2 does not copy, modify, or
    17	claim validation for them. Each later migration must pin its public tool and
    18	authorization contract, adopt the shared client/server surface, and add its own
    19	scenario and deployment evidence.
    20	
    21	Downstream Skillplane work consumes published McpFn packages after the guarded
    22	release sequence. This repository gate proves the shared packages, examples,
    23	packed external installation, and protocol fixtures; it does not prove a
    24	downstream deployment or hosted OAuth registration.
     1	# Testing and CI
     2	
     3	A regression-free MCP project needs five independent layers.
     4	
     5	| Layer | What it catches | McpFn surface |
     6	| --- | --- | --- |
     7	| Unit/domain | Handler logic, authorization, persistence, policy | Existing package tests |
     8	| Contract | Tools, resources, prompts, tasks, extensions, host requirements | Hashed manifest plus `mcpfn diff` |

    31	## Runtime ownership
    32	
    33	The official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` owns initialization, JSON-RPC dispatch, stdio framing, Streamable HTTP, capability negotiation, ping, and protocol errors. McpFn does not carry a second MCP protocol implementation.
    34	
    35	`McpFnServer` owns server identity, capability derivation, request-context construction, pagination, dispatch, error normalization, client-mediated roots/sampling/elicitation, notifications, and transport connection lifecycle. One `McpFnServer` instance connects to one transport. A host accepting multiple connections creates one server instance per connection while sharing the immutable registry.
    36	
    37	`McpFnRegistry` owns the application contract. It registers tools, exact resources, URI-template resources, prompts, completions, subscriptions, and task-capable tool handlers. Ajv validates tool and prompt inputs. URI templates are parsed once at registration. Task-capable tools require an explicit SDK `TaskStore`. MCP App links are validated across the full registry before a server or manifest is created.
    38	
    39	`McpFnServerDeclaration` is the side-effect-free application facade. It owns a
    40	registry, identity, transports, extensions, and client requirements; the same
    41	declaration creates manifests and per-connection server runtimes. Existing
    42	`McpFnServer` construction remains supported.
    43	
    44	## Client and session ownership
    45	
    46	`@mcpfn/client` owns target description, connection state, initialization,
    47	complete inventory pagination, tool/resource/prompt/task facades, explicit
    48	authorization callback completion, explicit reconnection, and bounded redacted
    49	diagnostics. It uses official SDK transports and protocol objects. It may retry
    50	connection establishment when configured; it never replays a caller's tool or
    51	other capability operation.
    52	
    53	The testing package wraps this production client for in-memory and external
    54	targets. The inspector records its diagnostics and invokes its facades. The CLI
    55	constructs its stdio or HTTP targets. This one-way dependency rule prevents
    56	test-only, inspector-only, or command-line protocol forks.
    57	
    58	## Authorization ownership
    59	
    60	The official SDK owns RFC discovery, DCR, PKCE construction, token exchange,
    61	refresh, and transport challenge handling. `@mcpfn/auth` supplies secure state
    62	and integration policy:
    63	
    64	- exact redirect matching with only the RFC 8252 loopback-port exception;
    65	- callback-state correlation before token exchange;
    66	- memory-only credentials by default or application-supplied encrypted storage;
    67	- redacted, bounded diagnostics and read-only discovery probes;
    68	- protected-resource verification and conversion to trusted SDK `authInfo`;
    69	- hosted metadata, registration, and authorization-request compatibility while
    70	  login, consent, signing, token issuance, and durable identity stay with the
    71	  host application.
    72	
    73	Client ID Metadata Document fetching is HTTPS-only, size-bounded, and requires
    74	an application allow-policy before any external URL is fetched. Additional
    75	advertised grant types do not invalidate a client that supports the requested
    76	authorization-code flow.
    77	
    78	## Manifest compatibility
    79	
    80	`createManifest` emits code-unit-sorted tool, resource, template, and prompt inventories plus a SHA-256 hash over a canonically ordered JSON representation. Object-valued capabilities, client requirements, and extensions retain their supplied insertion order in the returned body; their order does not affect the hash. `diffManifests` classifies changes as:
    81	
    82	- `breaking`: removed tools/properties/support, narrowed input enums, widened output enums, tighter input constraints, relaxed output constraints, newly required inputs, required output additions, and any output property added to a previously closed schema;
    83	- `additive`: added tools, optional input properties, optional output properties accepted by a previously open schema, widened input enums, relaxed input constraints, and added protocol/transport support;
    84	- `behavioral`: titles, descriptions, or annotations that can alter model tool selection without changing JSON validity.
    85	
    86	The diff is deliberately structural. Semantic scenarios are still required for authorization decisions, version resolution, idempotency, side effects, error envelopes, and result meaning.
    87	
    88	## DataFn integration
    89	
    90	`DatafnServer.executor` is an in-process boundary over the same query, mutation, transaction, and search handlers used by HTTP. It preserves authorization callbacks, namespace and actor derivation, schema permissions, plugins, rate limits, payload limits, and DataFn error envelopes.
    91	
    92	`@mcpfn/datafn` consumes that executor. It never accepts tenant, principal, namespace, or DataFn `clientId` values as tool arguments. Reads default on only after a resource is explicitly exposed; writes never default on.
    93	
    94	## Security invariants
    95	
    96	- Treat names, descriptions, annotations, schemas, and output shapes as versioned public contracts.
    97	- Build trusted context from the transport/authentication layer, not model-provided arguments.
    98	- Keep `additionalProperties: false` unless unknown keys are an intentional contract.
    99	- Prefer explicit output schemas for stable consumers.
   100	- Mark destructive and read-only annotations accurately; they influence client UX but do not replace server authorization.
   101	- Do not expose DataFn fields that its resolved read/write capabilities reject.
   102	- Require OAuth resource indicators and scopes at the HTTP boundary; never infer identity from model arguments.
   103	- Treat MCP Apps as untrusted HTML and declare the narrowest CSP and permissions.
   104	- Never write authorization codes, states, verifiers, tokens, cookies, or URL
   105	  credentials to diagnostic, inspection, or test artifacts.
